error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CONTROL DURING IN-FLIGHT PROFILE MODIFICATION

texts.0: SP, due to recomputing the route head-down with the aircraft left untrimmed, did not maintain the assigned leg altitude while modifying the mission profile. Altitude wandered more than 400 feet low and continued to decay toward the leg safety altitude without being detected. IP took control of the vertical flight path and levelled the aircraft before SP registered the deviation.
texts.1: SP, due to fixation on the navigation chart throughout the profile change, did not hold the assigned leg altitude. Altitude reached 300 feet off the cleared level and was recovered only after IP called the deviation twice from the rear cockpit. The correction came from verbal prompting alone and after several miles of track had been flown out of level.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction after the climb to the new leg altitude, allowed the aircraft to settle about 200 feet above the assigned level. SP detected the deviation on the next altimeter cross-check and re-established the level inside the following turn with no IP input. The remainder of the leg was flown within 150 feet.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude on every leg within 150 feet, including through the climb and descent segments imposed by the in-flight profile modification. Level-offs were anticipated and power was set so that no overshoot occurred. The altimeter cross-check stayed regular across the whole navigation.
texts.4: SP held every leg altitude to within a few tens of feet, including during the recomputed climb and descent segments required by the weather deviation. Each level-off was flown with the power lead point set correctly and no overshoot. Deviations from the planned vertical profile were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the leg altitudes within standards, but the deviations sat close to the upper edge of the tolerance and were consistently in the same direction, high after each climbing leg. The trend is toward a cross-check exercised after the altitude has already drifted rather than one that prevents the drift. SP is expected to tighten the altimeter scan during profile changes and hold the assigned level within half the tolerance on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the leg altitude while IP demonstrated the profile modification and called the altimeter scan needed through it, due to this being one of the first in-flight profile changes SP has flown holding a specific altitude through the modification. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to hold more of the altitude through a profile modification independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the assigned leg altitude while modifying the mission profile, holding the deviation to about 300 feet, at the edge of the standard, due to the altimeter scan being widened during the profile change rather than tightened. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to tighten the altimeter scan during profile changes, not widen it.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the assigned leg altitude while modifying the mission profile, holding the deviation to about 210 feet, due to the power setting after a climbing leg being confirmed a beat after the level-off rather than through it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm the power setting through the level-off, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the assigned leg altitude while modifying the mission profile, holding the deviation to about 150 feet, due to the level-off lead point being judged a fraction late during the climb segment. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to judge the level-off lead point earlier during the climb segment.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the assigned leg altitude while modifying the mission profile, holding the deviation to about 280 feet, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP maintained the assigned altitude on every leg to about 200 feet, including through the climb and descent segments imposed by the profile modification, level-offs anticipated with power set so no overshoot occurred. Judging the level-off lead point a fraction earlier during the climb would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good profile-altitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude on every leg to about 130 feet, including through the climb and descent segments required by the weather deviation, with the altimeter cross-check remaining regular across the whole navigation. The only refinement available was to hold that same lead through the steepest climb segment of the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good profile-altitude discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held every leg altitude to within a few tens of feet, including during the recomputed climb and descent segments required by the weather deviation, each level-off flown with the power lead point set correctly and no overshoot with deviations from the planned vertical profile negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent profile-altitude discipline.

error_modes.label: AIRSPEED CONTROL WHILE REVISING THE PROFILE

texts.0: SP, due to leaving the power lever at the transit setting while working on the revised route, did not maintain the planned leg airspeed. Speed decayed more than 25 knots below the planned value and the times SP had just recomputed became unusable within two legs. IP set the power and directed the airspeed back to the planned figure before the next turning point.
texts.1: SP, due to attention absorbed by the fuel recomputation, did not hold the planned leg airspeed. Airspeed reached 20 knots off the planned value and was restored only after IP prompted for a power check on the intercom. The correction was made on verbal direction alone and after the leg time had already run about a minute long.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected before the new altitude was established, first flew the revised leg about 15 knots fast. SP recognised the discrepancy at the leg midpoint, adjusted power and re-established the planned airspeed without IP intervention. The remaining legs were flown within 10 knots and the recomputed times held.
texts.3: SP maintained the planned leg airspeed within 10 knots throughout the navigation, including on the legs flown at the revised altitudes. Power was reset promptly after every altitude change so that ground speed matched the figures used for the in-flight recomputation. No airspeed correction was required from IP.
texts.4: SP flew each leg at the planned airspeed with deviations of only a few knots, resetting power immediately at every altitude and configuration change. The recomputed leg times were met to within seconds because the airspeed held exactly what the computation assumed. Deviations from the planned speed schedule were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP held the planned airspeed within standards, but each correction was applied late and the speed was allowed to drift toward the tolerance edge before being noticed. The trend is toward chasing the airspeed after a deviation has built rather than setting a known power value for the leg. SP is expected to use precomputed power settings for each altitude band and keep the leg airspeed inside half the tolerance next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the leg airspeed while IP called the power setting needed for the revised altitude band, due to this being one of the first profile revisions SP has flown resetting power for a newly computed altitude. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to reset more of the power independently for the revised altitude on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the planned leg airspeed while revising the profile, holding the deviation to about 20 knots, at the edge of the standard, due to the power setting being chosen from feel rather than from a precomputed value for the new altitude band. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to use the precomputed power value for the altitude band, not a setting chosen from feel.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the planned leg airspeed while revising the profile, holding the deviation to about 15 knots, due to the power setting being selected a beat before the new altitude was fully established. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to select the power setting only once the new altitude is fully established.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the planned leg airspeed while revising the profile, holding the deviation to about 10 knots, due to the airspeed being confirmed a fraction after the power change rather than in the same interval. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the airspeed in the same interval as the power change.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the planned leg airspeed while revising the profile, holding the deviation to about 18 knots, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP maintained the planned leg airspeed to about 15 knots throughout the navigation, including on the legs flown at the revised altitudes, power reset promptly after every altitude change so ground speed matched the figures used for the recomputation. Confirming the airspeed in the same interval as the power change, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound power-reset discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the planned leg airspeed to about 8 knots throughout the navigation, with no airspeed correction required from IP at any point of the revised profile. The only refinement available was to hold that same precomputed setting through the steepest altitude band change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed power-reset discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew each leg at the planned airspeed with deviations of only a few knots, resetting power immediately at every altitude and configuration change, the recomputed leg times met to within seconds because the airspeed held exactly what the computation assumed with deviations from the planned speed schedule negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional power-reset discipline.

error_modes.label: HEADING PRECISION ON THE REVISED TRACK

texts.0: SP, due to a heading computed from the wrong chart line during the in-flight amendment, did not fly the revised leg heading. The aircraft was flown more than 15 degrees off the required heading and diverged progressively from the intended ground track. IP had to give the correct heading to steer and monitor the roll-out onto it.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete compass cross-check after the turn onto the amended leg, did not hold the required heading. The aircraft settled 10 degrees off the computed heading and was corrected only after IP pointed out the discrepancy between the heading indicator and the planned value. The heading was regained on verbal prompting and after a noticeable delay.
texts.2: SP, due to rolling out early from the turn onto the new leg, initially held a heading about 8 degrees off the computed value. SP identified the error on the first heading cross-check, applied a measured correction and re-established the required heading without IP input. The rest of the leg was flown inside 5 degrees.
texts.3: SP flew each amended leg heading within 5 degrees of the computed value, rolling out on heading directly from every turn. Heading was cross-checked against the computed figure at each turning point and small corrections were applied immediately. No heading input was required from IP.
texts.4: SP rolled out on the exact computed heading at every turning point and held it with deviations of only one or two degrees for the whole leg. Heading, track and time stayed matched throughout the amended route with no accumulating error. Deviations from the planned heading schedule were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the required headings within standards, but corrections were made in large single inputs that overshot and then required a second correction back. The trend is toward heading control by successive overshoots rather than by small anticipated corrections. SP is expected to apply corrections proportional to the error and roll out on the computed heading directly in the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the amended leg heading with IP calling the computed heading and confirming the roll-out, due to this being one of the first in-flight amendments SP has flown rolling out on a heading computed during the sortie. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to confirm more of the computed heading independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP flew the amended leg heading within about 10 degrees of the computed value, at the edge of the standard, due to the correction being sized larger than the error before it was proportioned back. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to size every correction proportional to the error from the first input.
texts_at.2: SP flew the amended leg heading within about 7 degrees of the computed value, due to the compass cross-check after the turn being completed a beat after roll-out rather than as part of it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the compass cross-check as part of the roll-out, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP flew the amended leg heading within about 5 degrees of the computed value, due to the heading being confirmed against the computed figure a fraction after the turn rather than in the same motion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the heading against the computed figure in the same motion as the turn.

texts_above.1: SP flew the amended leg heading within about 9 degrees of the computed value, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew each amended leg heading to about 7 degrees of the computed value, rolling out on heading directly from every turn with heading cross-checked against the computed figure at each turning point and small corrections applied immediately. Confirming the heading against the computed figure in the same motion as the turn, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the roll-out further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid heading-correction discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew each amended leg heading to about 4 degrees of the computed value, with no heading input required from IP at any point of the revised route. The only refinement available was to hold that same precision through the sharpest amended turn. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed heading-correction discipline.
texts_above.4: SP rolled out on the exact computed heading at every turning point and held it with deviations of only one or two degrees for the whole leg, heading, track and time staying matched throughout the amended route with no accumulating error and deviations from the planned heading schedule negligible. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding heading-correction discipline.

error_modes.label: PROFILE MODIFICATION TO AVOID UNFAVOURABLE WEATHER

texts.0: SP, due to continuation of the plan after the information that invalidated it had already been received, did not modify the mission profile to avoid the unfavourable weather ahead. SP flew the briefed leg into deteriorating visibility with no alternative track prepared and no request to deviate. IP took control, turned the aircraft away from the weather and directed the modified profile.
texts.1: SP, due to continuation bias in maintaining the planned route after the conditions along it had clearly deteriorated, did not modify the mission profile in time. SP began the deviation only after IP had twice pointed out the cloud build-up on the leg. The profile was eventually modified safely but only through verbal direction and after the aircraft had closed to the edge of the usable visibility.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial deviation heading chosen without allowing for the extent of the cloud, first turned onto a track that would still have entered the affected area. SP reassessed the picture within the turn, selected a wider deviation and returned to the planned track after passing the weather, all without IP intervention. The modified profile kept the aircraft clear throughout.
texts.3: SP modified the mission profile appropriately to avoid the unfavourable weather encountered, selecting a deviation that kept the aircraft clear with a usable margin. The track was regained as soon as the affected area was passed and the sortie objectives were preserved. The modification was proposed and flown without prompting.
texts.4: SP recognised the developing weather well before it became a factor and modified the mission profile with a deviation that cost minimal time and fuel while keeping a generous margin from the affected area. The return to the planned track was flown at the earliest safe point and the recomputed times were already available when the track was regained. Deviations from the ideal solution were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP modified the profile within standards, but the decision was taken only when the weather had become an immediate factor rather than while options were still open. The trend is toward reacting to conditions at the last usable moment instead of deciding at a named decision point. SP is expected to set explicit deviation criteria before each leg and act on them as soon as they are met.

texts_at.0: SP modified the profile to avoid the weather with IP naming the deviation criterion and confirming the new heading, due to this being one of the first weather deviations SP has flown deciding and flying a modified profile in flight. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to name more of the deviation criteria independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP modified the mission profile to avoid the unfavourable weather encountered, due to the deviation criterion for that leg being named only as the weather became an immediate factor rather than before the leg began. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to name the deviation criterion before the leg begins, not as the weather closes in.
texts_at.2: SP modified the mission profile to avoid the unfavourable weather encountered, due to the decision being taken a beat after the named criterion was met rather than as it was met. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to act on the named criterion the moment it is met, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP modified the mission profile to avoid the unfavourable weather encountered, due to the deviation heading being confirmed a fraction after the decision rather than in the same step. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the deviation heading in the same step as the decision.

texts_above.1: SP modified the mission profile to avoid the unfavourable weather encountered. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP modified the mission profile appropriately to avoid the unfavourable weather encountered, selecting a deviation that kept the aircraft clear with a usable margin, the track regained as soon as the affected area was passed with the modification proposed and flown without prompting. Confirming the deviation heading in the same step as the decision, rather than a fraction after, would sharpen the response further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady weather-decision discipline.
texts_above.3: SP modified the mission profile with a deviation costing minimal time and fuel while keeping a generous margin from the affected area, the recomputed times already available when the track was regained. The only refinement available was to name that same decision point a leg earlier still. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate weather-decision discipline.
texts_above.4: SP recognised the developing weather well before it became a factor and modified the mission profile with a deviation that cost minimal time and fuel while keeping a generous margin from the affected area, the return to the planned track flown at the earliest safe point with the recomputed times already available when the track was regained. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary weather-decision discipline.

error_modes.label: IN-FLIGHT FUEL, TIME AND DISTANCE COMPUTATION

texts.0: SP, due to using the planned ground speed instead of the actual one after the deviation, did not compute fuel in flight correctly against time and distance. The fuel remaining figure SP reported for the turning point was wrong by a margin that would have concealed a shortfall on the return leg. IP recomputed fuel, time and distance and issued the corrected figures to SP.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted fuel check that was never completed, did not produce the in-flight fuel and time figures at the turning point. SP arrived at the correct numbers only after IP prompted for each element in turn, fuel remaining, time to run and distance to go. The computation reached the minimum acceptable standard solely through verbal guidance and well after the turning point.
texts.2: SP, due to reading the wrong leg line on the flight log, first computed a time to the next turning point that was inconsistent with the fuel used. SP noticed the mismatch during the routine fuel check, recomputed from the correct leg and had valid figures before the turning point, without IP input. Fuel and time were then tracked correctly for the remainder of the sortie.
texts.3: SP computed fuel in flight precisely in relation to time and distance, updating the figures at every turning point and after the profile modification. The fuel remaining at each check matched the computed value and the reserve was tracked against the planned minimum. No computation required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuously updated fuel, time and distance picture, recomputing immediately after the deviation and cross-checking the result against actual fuel flow. Every turning point figure was available before the aircraft reached it and matched the indicated fuel to within a few pounds. Errors in the in-flight computation were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP computed fuel, time and distance within standards, but the checks were done only at the turning points and the figures were carried forward without allowance for the changed ground speed. The trend is toward computations that are formally correct yet lag the actual state of the aircraft. SP is expected to update the fuel and time picture whenever speed, altitude or track changes, not only at fixed points.

texts_at.0: SP computed fuel in flight with IP calling the time and distance figures needed after the profile change, due to this being one of the first in-flight fuel computations SP has updated against a revised profile rather than the original plan. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to update more of the fuel computation independently after a profile change on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP computed fuel in flight precisely in relation to time and distance, due to the figure being carried forward unchanged after a speed change rather than updated at the change itself. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to update the fuel and time picture at every speed change, not only at fixed points.
texts_at.2: SP computed fuel in flight precisely in relation to time and distance, due to the update after the profile modification being made a beat after the change rather than with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to update the picture in the same step as the profile modification.
texts_at.3: SP computed fuel in flight precisely in relation to time and distance, due to the figure at one turning point being logged a fraction after the check rather than at it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to log the figure at the checkpoint itself, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP computed fuel in flight precisely in relation to time and distance. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP computed fuel in flight precisely in relation to time and distance, updating the figures at every turning point and after the profile modification with the fuel remaining at each check matching the computed value. Logging the figure at the checkpoint itself, rather than a fraction after, would keep the picture consistently current. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable fuel-time-currency discipline.
texts_above.3: SP computed fuel in flight precisely in relation to time and distance, no computation requiring correction by IP with the reserve tracked against the planned minimum throughout. The only refinement available was to update the picture a step earlier after the fastest speed change of the sortie. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good fuel-time-currency discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a continuously updated fuel, time and distance picture, recomputing immediately after the deviation and cross-checking the result against actual fuel flow, every turning point figure available before the aircraft reached it and matching the indicated fuel to within a few pounds with errors in the in-flight computation negligible. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior fuel-time-currency discipline.

error_modes.label: IN-FLIGHT AMENDMENT OF THE FLIGHT PLAN

texts.0: SP, due to amending the flight plan without re-reading the entries back against the chart, made errors in the in-flight modification. The revised leg sequence contained a turning point that no longer matched the track flown and the revised ETAs were carried over from the original plan. IP had to stop the amendment, correct the log and dictate the valid sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to attempting the flight plan amendment while simultaneously flying the turn, entered the revised legs with errors in headings and times. The log was made usable only after IP identified each incorrect entry from the rear cockpit. The amendment was completed on verbal prompting and after the aircraft had already passed the affected turning point.
texts.2: SP, due to writing the revised heading before the new distance had been measured, first entered an inconsistent leg on the flight log. SP cross-checked the entry against the chart, corrected the heading and time and had a coherent amended plan before the turn, with no IP intervention. The remaining amendments were entered correctly at the first attempt.
texts.3: SP modified the flight plan in flight without making mistakes, entering revised headings, distances, times and fuel figures that were consistent with each other and with the chart. Each amendment was completed before the aircraft reached the affected turning point. The log remained legible and usable throughout the sortie.
texts.4: SP amended the flight plan in flight with complete accuracy and without interrupting aircraft control, producing revised headings, times and fuel figures that were cross-checked against the chart as they were written. The amended log was complete before the aircraft reached the deviation point and required no further change. Errors in the amendment were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP amended the flight plan within standards, but each entry was written and then reworked once, and the log became difficult to read at the amended legs. The trend is toward an amendment process that produces a correct final answer through repeated correction rather than at the first attempt. SP is expected to measure and confirm each element before writing it, and to keep the amended log legible for later use.

texts_at.0: SP amended the flight plan with IP calling each revised heading, distance and time for SP to enter, due to this being one of the first in-flight amendments SP has entered onto the flight plan while airborne. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to enter more of the amended figures independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP modified the flight plan in flight without making mistakes, due to one entry being written before the distance behind it was measured rather than after. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to measure every element before writing it, not write and then measure.
texts_at.2: SP modified the flight plan in flight without making mistakes, due to one heading being cross-checked against the chart a beat after it was written rather than as it was written. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to cross-check every heading against the chart as it is written, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP modified the flight plan in flight without making mistakes, due to one entry being reworked once for legibility rather than written clearly the first time. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to write every entry clearly the first time, not rework it for legibility.

texts_above.1: SP modified the flight plan in flight without making mistakes. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP modified the flight plan in flight without making mistakes, entering revised headings, distances, times and fuel figures that were consistent with each other and with the chart, each amendment completed before the aircraft reached the affected turning point. Writing every entry clearly the first time, rather than reworking it, would keep the log legible throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured flight-plan-amendment discipline.
texts_above.3: SP modified the flight plan in flight without making mistakes, the log remaining legible and usable throughout the sortie with no entry requiring rework. The only refinement available was to hold that same first-attempt accuracy through the busiest amendment of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise flight-plan-amendment discipline.
texts_above.4: SP amended the flight plan in flight with complete accuracy and without interrupting aircraft control, producing revised headings, times and fuel figures that were cross-checked against the chart as they were written, the amended log complete before the aircraft reached the deviation point with errors in the amendment negligible. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate flight-plan-amendment discipline.

error_modes.label: SAFETY ALTITUDE, OBSTACLE CLEARANCE AND VFR ALTITUDE RULES

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of a published restriction that was available in the briefing material, did not modify the flight altitude so that minimum altitudes with respect to obstacles were preserved. SP descended for the weather deviation below the leg safety altitude and was unable to state the RAA or the safety altitude for the leg when asked. IP arrested the descent and directed a climb back to a legal and safe level.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of awareness of the terrain profile on the amended leg, did not apply the correct safety altitude to the modified route. The aircraft was levelled at an altitude that met the leg minimum only after IP stated the required figure. SP recalled the semicircular rule and the affected airport altitudes only when prompted item by item.
texts.2: SP, due to applying the safety altitude of the original leg to the amended one, initially selected a level that was correct for terrain but not for the semicircular rule on the new heading. SP identified the discrepancy while writing the amendment, climbed to the correct VFR level and confirmed the leg safety altitude, without IP input. Obstacle clearance was preserved at every stage.
texts.3: SP modified the flight altitude so that minimum altitudes with respect to obstacles were never violated and the level flown complied with the semicircular rule for the heading in use. SP stated the safety altitude for each leg and the RAA when asked, and accounted for the altitudes affecting the nearby airports. No altitude selection required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP had the safety altitude of every leg, the RAA and the altitude limits imposed by the nearby airports available without reference to notes, and applied them immediately when the profile was modified. Each amended level satisfied terrain clearance, the semicircular rule and the airport constraints simultaneously and was selected before the turn onto the leg. Errors of altitude selection were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitudes legal and clear of obstacles within standards, but the leg safety altitude and the RAA were recalled only after a pause and by reading them from the log. The trend is toward altitude limits that are looked up rather than held actively while the profile is being changed. SP is expected to carry the leg safety altitudes, the RAA and the affected airport altitudes as ready knowledge on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP modified the flight altitude with IP naming the leg safety altitude and the semicircular rule figure to apply, due to this being one of the first profile modifications SP has flown selecting a legal altitude in flight rather than from the plan. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to name more of the safety altitude and rule figures independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP modified the flight altitude so minimum altitudes with respect to obstacles were never violated, due to the leg safety altitude being read from the log after a pause rather than recalled as ready knowledge. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to carry the leg safety altitude as ready knowledge, not read it from the log after a pause.
texts_at.2: SP modified the flight altitude so minimum altitudes with respect to obstacles were never violated, due to the RAA being confirmed a beat after the safety altitude rather than in the same recall. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to recall the RAA in the same breath as the safety altitude, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP modified the flight altitude so minimum altitudes with respect to obstacles were never violated, due to the semicircular rule being applied a fraction after the level was selected rather than as part of selecting it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to apply the semicircular rule as part of selecting the level, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP modified the flight altitude so minimum altitudes with respect to obstacles were never violated. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP modified the flight altitude so that minimum altitudes with respect to obstacles were never violated and the level flown complied with the semicircular rule, the safety altitude for each leg and the RAA stated when asked with no altitude selection requiring correction by IP. Applying the semicircular rule as part of selecting the level, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the recall further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent safety-altitude recall.
texts_above.3: SP modified the flight altitude so obstacle clearance, the semicircular rule and the airport constraints were satisfied simultaneously, the leg safety altitude and the RAA carried as ready knowledge throughout. The only refinement available was to hold that same ready recall through the busiest profile change of the route. error_modes.label: LEVEL OFF POWER AND PLANNED FUEL FLOW ON THE NEW LEG

texts.0: SP, due to reducing power at level off instead of keeping climb power until approaching the planned IAS, did not establish the new leg at the mission planned airspeed. Airspeed settled more than 20 knots below plan, the planned fuel flow was never set and the leg times just recomputed for the revised profile were invalidated. IP set the power and the fuel flow and directed the recomputation of the leg.
texts.1: SP, due to setting the PCL by feel rather than to the planned fuel flow after the climb to the new leg altitude, allowed the airspeed to stabilise 20 knots off the mission planned IAS. The power was corrected and the fuel flow set only after IP called the airspeed twice. The planned IAS was restored through verbal prompting and after several miles of the amended leg had been flown.
texts.2: SP, due to a late transition from climb power to the planned fuel flow at level off, allowed the airspeed to overshoot the mission planned IAS by about 15 knots. SP recognised the trend on the airspeed indicator, adjusted the PCL to the planned fuel flow and stabilised the leg with no IP input. The later level-offs were flown within 10 knots.
texts.3: SP kept climb power until approaching the planned IAS at level off and then set the planned fuel flow to hold the airspeed on each amended leg. Airspeed was maintained within 10 knots of the mission planned IAS and the PCL was adjusted as required when the altitude or the winds changed. The leg times of the revised profile remained valid.
texts.4: SP levelled off on each new leg with the power lead point judged so that the aircraft accelerated directly to the mission planned IAS, then held it on the planned fuel flow. Airspeed excursions were of a few knots and the fuel flow matched the figure used for the revised leg times. Deviations from the planned airspeed profile were negligible.

The trend is toward a leg that stabilises late, which distorts the leg times and the fuel figures just recomputed. SP is expected to use the planned fuel flow as the reference setting at every level off on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: CONTINUATION FUEL AND EARLY ROUTE TERMINATION DECISION

texts.0: SP, due to having no continuation fuel figure computed for the checkpoints of the revised route, did not recognise that the fuel required to continue and reach the landing destination with reserves would be exceeded. SP pressed on along the amended track with the reserve unprotected and no decision point identified. IP terminated the route and directed the aircraft direct to the final checkpoint.
texts.1: SP, due to a continuation fuel computed only for the original route and never reworked backwards for the amended legs, had no usable minimum fuel figure at the checkpoints. SP accepted that the route had to be shortened only after IP presented the arithmetic. The decision to proceed direct to the final checkpoint was taken on IP direction rather than on SP's own fuel check.
texts.2: SP, due to omitting the transit fuel from the end of the route to the landing destination when the profile was revised, initially derived a continuation fuel that was optimistic at the last two checkpoints. SP reworked the computation backwards from the destination with reserves, corrected the figures and shortened the route at the next checkpoint with no IP input.
texts.3: SP computed continuation fuel for the revised route by working backwards from the landing destination with reserves through each amended leg, and compared the fuel remaining against that minimum at every checkpoint. The route was modified in good time as the fuel to continue was approached, proceeding direct to the final checkpoint as expected. No fuel decision required IP direction.
texts.4: SP carried a continuation fuel figure for every checkpoint of the amended route, including the transit from the end of the route to the landing destination, and compared it against the actual fuel at each crossing. The decision to shorten the route was identified well before the fuel to continue was reached and was stated with the supporting figures. Departures from the planned fuel profile were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the continuation fuel figures within standards, but they were reworked only at the checkpoints where IP asked for the fuel state and the margin was allowed to close before any decision was voiced. The trend is toward a fuel decision taken at the limit rather than at a planned decision point. SP is expected to work continuation fuel backwards for the whole amended route as soon as the profile changes.

The check was continued through a formation turn rather than suspended and resumed afterwards. IP took control to re-establish deconfliction and position before the check was completed.

The check was interrupted and the position restored only on direction from the rear cockpit, and the check-in was transmitted without call sign and total fuel until prompted. The check reached the minimum acceptable standard through verbal prompting.

SP stopped the check, flew the formation through the turn and resumed the remaining items one at a time with a position check between each, transmitting call sign and total fuel correctly. No IP input was required.

The check was suspended for the turn and resumed once the turn was complete, and the check-in was transmitted with call sign and total fuel. Position and deconfliction were maintained throughout.

Departures from the briefed position during the checks were negligible.

SP is expected to take one item at a time and to check position between each item on the next sortie.

Bingo was reached before any fuel state was transmitted and the recovery had to be started at once. IP directed the fuel call and the recovery decision.

SP is expected to increase the frequency of the fuel checks during high fuel flow operations on the next sortie.
